claims.text: You are about to explore the Palais Lascaris in Nice, where a remarkable collection awaits.
Encounter the Violes gambe by William Turner, the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, and the Harpe by Naderman.
Each work showcases the transformation of musical expression in Europe through craftsmanship and innovation.
Testore's 1696 bass viol, part of the historical musical instrument collection transferred to the Palais Lascaris in 2001, sets the stage for a journey through time and musical evolution.
Your first stop is Violes gambe by William Turner (Londres, 1652).
As you stand in the Palais Lascaris, let your gaze fall upon the viola da gamba crafted by William Turner in 1652.
This position allows you to see the delicate artistry that reflects not just Turner's skill but also the turbulent times of its creation.
Turner, primarily known as a painter in London, extended his artistry to the intricate design of violas da gamba during a period of English Civil War uncertainty.
His violas, distinguished by their heart-shaped contours, are not merely instruments; they symbolize the resilience and cultural continuity of England during tumultuous times.
The Palais Lascaris now stands as the second most important historical musical instrument collection, surpassed only by the Musée de la Musique in Paris.

The presence of this instrument within the Palais connects its audience not only to the annals music but also to a shared European cultural heritage, emphasizing the palace's mission to preserve and celebrate these ancient sounds.

claims.text: Consider how each crafted element of the Basse de violon, from its robust body to the elegant scrollwork, was designed to balance aesthetic beauty with acoustic performance.
This harp is not just a musical instrument but a window into the elegance of the late 18th century—a time of opulence and sophistication in France.
Jean-Henri Naderman, active as a celebrated harp maker in Paris from at least 1735 to 1799, specialized in crafting harps that were both aesthetically beautiful and functionally advanced.
The harp is made from painted and gilded wood and metal, reflecting the grandeur of pre-Revolutionary France.
The instrument, once belonging to the Viscountess of Beaumont, was more than just a beautiful artifact.
In December 2008, this same harp was brought to a studio for gold restoration, preserving its historical splendor.
